title: Aftercare
description: Astrology, tarot, and a journal, as an Expo app, a Netlify web app, and an Astro site. The plan was a Dawn profile.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Aftercare is astrology, tarot, and a journal. The README on Artometrics/aftercare calls it "soft guidance for your inner life." The repo was still readable on 14 Nov 2026. The archive index says not to delete it until a Dawn merge exists. The host named for the Astro app is aftercare-510519.web.app. The Netlify app is aftercare-artometrics.netlify.app.

What it was

Three surfaces in one repo.

The root is an Expo app. package.json names Expo ~57, Expo Router, React Native 0.86, and Nativewind. app.json is present. The README says this native app is for a later release, and that web is the live surface.

web/ is the Netlify app, deployed from main with netlify.toml (base = web). The README lists Netlify Identity, a private journal with mood tags in Netlify Database, tarot spreads with an AI interpretation and Gemini card art cached in Blobs, daily mood check-ins with a chart, birth profile tools (sun sign, life path, next birthday, moon), and a daily home with a sky note.

site/ is a separate local-first Astro app: a three.js tarot table, numerology, and a shareable "second self" profile. PR #6 (10 Nov 2026) is the commit that adds that MVP. PR #7 gives site/ its own Firebase project, aftercare-510519, with noindex, and leaves the Netlify app alone. PR #8 adds a GitHub Actions deploy of site/ to that Hosting site.

Why it was built

The README's line is the brief: astrology, tarot, and journaling. The archive index's destination is more specific. Clicking your profile in Dawn should show Aftercare. That is the fold that was written down. The repo does not, on its own, say why Dawn was the home. The index does.

How it worked

Expo at the root for the phone app. Astro and three.js in site/ for the tarot table. Netlify Identity, Netlify Database, and Blobs in web/ for the account, the journal, and the card art. Schema for the web database is web/db/schema.ts. Migrations live under web/netlify/database/migrations/.

Local web dev is cd web && npm install && npm run dev. The README says Identity does not fully work in local-only mode until the site has been deployed once, and points at npx netlify dev for auth. The Astro site is the Firebase target. Offline, the index says on-device data should work once the app is built. I am not restating emulator passwords. The inventory omitted those on purpose.

What I learned

Aftercare grew a second and third app instead of picking one. The Netlify app has the account and the journal. The Astro app has the 3D table and the shareable profile. The Expo app is still the root package.json. The archive note treats the thing Dawn should open as "Aftercare," singular. The repo is three codebases. Any merge has to say which one.

A smaller note from the history: on 22 Jul 2026 a commit replaced a top nav that spilled past the phone with a five-tab bottom bar. The layout problem showed up before the Astro rewrite.

Where it went

Dawn, as a profile, in the archive plan. The repo was still separate on 14 Nov 2026. A code search of Artometrics/dawn for aftercare returned no matches. GitHub marked that search incomplete. The index says to keep the repo until that merge exists. The Drive folder is a copy, not a replacement.

Download the archive

Folder: Aftercare.

The index says four files in the folder matched local sizes on 13 Nov 2026 at 8:29 PM PT. The repo itself is the fuller history: Artometrics/aftercare.

Sources

  • Artometrics/aftercare README and root package.json, read 14 Nov 2026
  • Commits 1f247fc5 (22 Jul 2026, bottom nav), a76898cb (PR #6), 7616fbb8 (PR #7), a19c6dc8 (PR #8)
  • Artometrics Archive Index, Aftercare row
  • Code search of Artometrics/dawn on 14 Nov 2026

title: Carrie
description: Carrie's suite: PageMatch for books, PawCert for pets, and a portal. Books were filed for Dawn. Pets were filed for Bagel. The repo was still up.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Carrie is a web suite Carrie made, hosted as three Firebase sites in the Artometrics org. The README on Artometrics/carrie names them: PageMatch at carrie-books.web.app, PawCert Studio at carrie-pets.web.app, and a portal at carrie-510519.web.app. The repo was still readable on 14 Nov 2026. The latest commit on main that day, a7345400, adds noindex for all three sites (an X-Robots-Tag header and robots.txt).

This Carrie is the suite. Carrie Scott's portfolio is a different site, carrie-scott-portfolio.web.app, and the archive index says to keep that one. It is not this report.

What it was

Two apps and a front door.

PageMatch is a book quiz. The README describes five questions (reading vibe, genre, pacing and length, tropes, and what you want out of the book), a score against a library it calls "35+ acclaimed bestsellers," match reasons, Amazon affiliate buttons (default tag carrie-20, changeable in settings), a shelf in local storage, search, genre filters, and a dark and light theme.

PawCert Studio makes pet certificates: birth, gotcha day or adoption, a milestone birthday, a "100% good pet" honor, and a royal-companion joke. Fields are the pet's name, species, breed, dates, pronouns, guardian names, hometown, a registration number, a motto, and a photo in a round frame or a species silhouette. Four themes are named: classic gold, sage ivy, birthday confetti, and royal midnight. Export is a canvas PNG at 2400 by 1700, plus print CSS for US Letter or A4 landscape. Sample presets are a golden retriever, a calico, a French bulldog, and a beagle.

The portal is portal/index.html, a landing page between the two.

A commit on 6 Oct 2026, 8835e4f6, says it adds Literary Tarot, a Gutenberg press vault, CliffNotes capsules, and a one-screen PawCert studio. The README on main, read 14 Nov 2026, describes PageMatch and PawCert and does not repeat those names. I am not inventing how the tarot or the vault behaved beyond that commit message.

Why it was built

The README says Carrie made it: a book matchmaker and a certificate for a pet. The archive index's later plan is about where the pieces live, not about replacing that. Books go to Dawn. Pets go to Bagel. The repo is retired only after both merges. The index also says to ask Carrie before taking the live sites down.

How it worked

Vite, one app per folder: apps/books, apps/pets, and portal. package.json name is carrie-suite. Scripts are dev:books on port 3000, dev:pets on 3001, dev:portal on 3002. The production dependency list in that file is vite and canvas-confetti. Deploy is firebase-tools against project carrie-510519, with hosting targets books, pets, and portal. npm run deploy builds all three and deploys them together.

The first commit, 6 Oct 2026, 5715938e, is the initial PageMatch and PawCert release.

What I learned

The suite was already split, which makes the archive plan literal. Books and pets do not have to move together. They already deploy as different Hosting sites. The open question is the one the index wrote down: do not delete the repo, and do not take Carrie's sites down, until Dawn has the books and Bagel has the pets. The code search on 14 Nov 2026 did not show those landings, and GitHub marked it incomplete.

Where it went

Books into Dawn, pets into Bagel, as the recorded plan. On 14 Nov 2026 a code search of Artometrics/dawn for PageMatch, and of Artometrics/bagel for PawCert, pets, and carrie, returned no matches. GitHub marked those searches incomplete. The Carrie repo was still its own repo. The Drive folder is the copy for when that retire happens. It has not happened.

Download the archive

Folder: Carrie.

The index says four files matched local sizes on 13 Nov 2026 at 8:29 PM PT, and that Artometrics--carrie.bundle in the GitHub remainder set covers the repo again. The live repo is Artometrics/carrie.

Sources

  • Artometrics/carrie README and package.json, read 14 Nov 2026
  • Commits 5715938e, 8835e4f6, and a7345400 (PR #1, noindex)
  • Artometrics Archive Index, "Carrie (Books, Pets, hub)" row
  • Code search of Artometrics/dawn and Artometrics/bagel on 14 Nov 2026

title: CRM
description: A private contacts and deal board for Artometrics. The plan was to fold it into Dawn and keep the Firebase project.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
CRM was a private Artometrics desk for people, companies, deals, notes, and follow-ups. There was no GitHub remote. The archive index points at the box tree /workspace/crm-dep, and the live host was crm-510519.web.app.

What it was

An internal pipeline, not a public product. The 13 Nov 2026 inventory calls the code solid: rules tests, emulators, and a PWA, with no web API key baked into the client.

Why it was built

The inventory's reason is the feature list. I wanted one place for contacts and a deal board, with a Today view for tasks, instead of another spreadsheet.

How it worked

React, Vite, and TypeScript, on Firebase project crm-510519. The inventory lists contacts, companies, a kanban with Lead, Contacted, Proposal, Won, and Lost, notes, Today tasks, global search, CSV import and export, phone quick-add, offline persistence, allowlisted Google and Apple sign-in, and Storage attachments. Firestore (default) was present. Secrets were left out of the zip.

Offline: npm install && npm run build, then serve dist/. Auth and Firestore need the emulators.

What I learned

A small CRM with emulator tests and rules tests was further along than several louder apps. The inventory's recommendation was to merge it into Dawn as a contacts and pipeline desk, disable Hosting only, and keep the Firebase project because Firestore was there. The index does not record that the project was deleted.

Where it went

The recorded destination is Dawn, as a contacts and pipeline desk. Dawn itself was not changed on 13 Nov 2026. The inventory says so in its first paragraph. The standalone source is the Drive zip.

Download the archive

crm-archive.zip (590,771 bytes, SHA-256 be7b189c47dc0401ad110783fe216d75b3e860376c8fa5c7619bc9cbcdacb5b8). The same folder holds the working-tree zip and the live mirror as separate files, listed in SUMMARY.json.

Folder: Unlisted sites 2026-11-13.

Sources

title: Fernbound
description: A canvas game meant to become a Dawn hunt for nearby spirits. No GitHub repo. The box tree is the source.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Fernbound was a canvas game. The Drive README says it is to be merged into Dawn as a Pokémon-style feature: hunt real monsters and spirits from history near you. The host was fernbound-510519.web.app. There is no GitHub repo. The source named in the README is /workspace/fernbound-deploy.

What it was

A small static web game, 11 files in the working-tree zip, and a much larger byte count (11,981,445) than the file count suggests. The KSM inventory, from before this archive, could only verify the page title. The 13 Nov README is the description I am using.

Why it was built

The README states the Dawn feature, not a studio backstory. Walk near where you are, and meet a spirit that belongs to that place. The index says that decision was already made, and that the box copy should not be deleted until the Dawn merge exists.

How it worked

Canvas, static web, Firebase Hosting. Offline, serve public/ with python3 -m http.server. No git history was available. The package is the working-tree zip and a live mirror (95,381 bytes).

What I learned

Eleven files can still be a game if the art is most of the zip. The merge instruction is the part worth keeping: do not throw out the only copy before Dawn has the hunt. On 13 Nov the inventory says Dawn was not changed.

Where it went

Dawn, as a planned fold. On 14 Nov 2026 a code search of Artometrics/dawn for fernbound returned no matches. GitHub marked that search incomplete, so the miss is not proof the name is absent. title: Lineage
description: A browser battle for Cannae, Austerlitz, and Waterloo. The archive says merge it into Pantheon and keep the repo.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Lineage is a historical battle you play in the browser. The README on Artometrics/lineage calls it a Napoleonic battle sim and says to pick Cannae, Austerlitz, or Waterloo. The title screen in public/index.html is wider than that README: Alexander at Gaugamela and Caesar at Alesia are locked buttons, and Cannae, Austerlitz, and Waterloo are the playable chapters. The host in the README and in DEPLOY.md is lineage-waterloo.web.app, on Firebase project artometrics-510519. The page ships noindex.

The repo was still readable on 14 Nov 2026. The archive index says not to delete the repo or the site.

What it was

A phase-by-phase battle, tap or click, with a command map. Waterloo is public/game.js (and three.module.js vendored next to it). Austerlitz is public/austerlitz.js. Cannae is public/cannae.js. Specs live in docs/AUSTERLITZ_SPEC.md, docs/CANNAE_SPEC.md, and docs/ROADMAP_UNREAL.md. Python files test.py, test_cannae.py, test_v2.py, and test_v3.py sit at the repo root. Screenshot PNGs are committed at the root and under shots-v2/ and shots-v3/. This report does not describe those images.

Why it was built

The title screen says "Play the great commanders. Give the real orders." The commits say the same thing in smaller pieces. Waterloo v1 was the baseline deployed 25 Oct 2026. Austerlitz became a chapter the same day. Cannae arrived on 9 Nov 2026 as a chapter about giving ground: Hannibal holds the centre, the crescent bends, the Africans turn inward. A follow-up the same day sets the end screen to Livy 22.49 (45,500 foot and 2,700 horse) and keeps Britannica's 55,000 as a note. PR #3 on 10 Nov adds an opt-in Livy dust view and a drier Roman cold open.

The 13 Nov archive row still says "Cannae is roadmap-only." The repo disagrees, and the Cannae commits are older than that row. I am treating the README, index.html, and those commits as the current fact. The index row is the merge plan, and it is stale on Cannae.

How it worked

Vanilla JavaScript and Three.js, same pairing the archive index notes for Pantheon. Firebase Hosting of public/. Controls, from the title screen: WASD or arrows, or the left stick. Act with E or Space. Map with M. Sound toggle on the page.

DEPLOY.md creates the Hosting site lineage-waterloo on project artometrics-510519 and deploys hosting:lineage-waterloo. Offline, serve public/ over HTTP.

The index's suggested landing inside Pantheon is site/lineage/. On 14 Nov 2026 a code search of Artometrics/pantheon for "lineage" returned no matches. GitHub marked that search incomplete. The Pantheon README I read the same day describes Pantheon's own fighter (Arcade, Story, Versus, Training) and does not mention Lineage.

What I learned

The playable part got ahead of the archive sentence. Cannae was a chapter with a cited death toll before the index called it a roadmap. The locked chapters are honest about that: Alexander and Alesia are on the title screen and disabled. The Unreal roadmap doc is a doc. The thing that runs is the browser build.

The merge target is Pantheon, not Dawn. Both are vanilla JS and Three.js, which is the reason the index gives.

Where it went

Pantheon, as a planned merge. The repo and the Waterloo host were to stay until that merge exists. As of 14 Nov 2026 the Lineage repo was still its own repo. The Pantheon code search returned no hit and was marked incomplete. The Drive folder is the copy if the repo is retired later. It has not been retired.

Download the archive

Folder: Lineage.

The index says six files in that folder matched local sizes on 13 Nov 2026 at 8:29 PM PT. The git bundle is not in this folder. It is in the GitHub remainder set as three parts, Artometrics--lineage.bundle.part-00 through part-02. The folder README there is described as an older copy.

Repo, still up when this was written: Artometrics/lineage.

Sources

title: Loom
description: A YouTube cut board: script, captions, and a transcriber. It does not download YouTube. The host was deleted after the zip.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Loom was a YouTube studio board. Topic or article URL in. Script, narration notes, picture notes, captions, title, description, and thumbnail concepts out. The inventory is explicit that it does not download YouTube. No GitHub repo. The box path was /workspace/loom-dep. The host was loom-510519.web.app.

What it was

A desk for cutting a video down to a package, plus a transcriber for uploaded recordings and a list of sources with their licenses. The inventory calls it Kyle's YouTube studio board.

Why it was built

A studio that writes also has to package a video. The 13 Nov note says Loom is useful if Dawn is that studio, and that it was less urgent than Newsletter or invoicing.

How it worked

Next.js PWA, Cloud Functions, an MCP surface, and emulator tests, on Firebase project loom-510519. The live site could still say the back end was not enabled if the functions had never been deployed. Script writing works locally without a cloud key. Offline, npm run dev against the emulators.

The delete row says Firestore was empty, the project delete was requested at 8:22 PM PT on 13 Nov 2026, and the host was 404.

What I learned

The useful boundary was the one already written down: do not download YouTube. A transcriber for a file I uploaded, and a package of titles and captions, was the whole tool. The merge could wait.

Where it went

Retired. The inventory's alternate was a later Dawn "YouTube cut" board. That merge was not done on 13 Nov. The zip is the source if it happens later.

title: Magazine mockup
description: An Artometrics magazine front end on its own host. The mockup was retired. artometrics.com stayed.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
The magazine mockup was an Artometrics Magazine front end on artometrics-mag-510519.web.app. The Drive README describes it as 103 issues and 5-minute reads, and says it may overlap the real magazine on artometrics.com. No GitHub remote is listed. Sources were /workspace/mag-src.zip and the box tree /workspace/artomag.

What it was

A mock of the magazine, not the magazine. The decision, recorded at 6:25 PM PT on 13 Nov 2026, was to retire the mockup and leave artometrics.com up.

Why it was built

The README frames it as a front end for the issues. A separate host let the mock move without touching the live magazine. Once the real site was the magazine, the mock host was a second copy.

Offline, serve artomag/public or artomag/site, or unzip mag-src.zip and run npm install and npm run dev. Shots were included. The README says artomag/shots is about 142 MB.

The index says the working tree is stored as two parts plus the checksum, and that the host was deleted at 6:38 PM PT.

A mock on its own Firebase site starts to look like a product. The decision at 6:25 PM was to keep one magazine. The shots are large, and they belong in the zip, not on a second public host.

title: Mia Maps
description: A Craigslist rental hunter for Mia. The hourly scrape was still running when the archive was packed.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Mia Maps was a San Francisco rental hunter for Mia. The 13 Nov 2026 feature inventory describes it as a Craigslist scrape, a score for neighborhoods and amenities, a listing tracker in SQLite and Excel, drafted landlord notes, and an email digest.

What it was

A personal rental desk. The host was mia-rentals-510519.web.app. The repo named in the archive index is Artometrics/mia-maps. On 14 Nov 2026 that GitHub path was not visible from this account. The Drive package still holds a git bundle, so the history is in the zip even if the remote is gone.

Why it was built

The inventory states the job in one line: find rentals for Mia. It is filed as archive-only, and the same note says it is not a Dawn feature.

How it worked

The code the inventory describes is a Python pipeline. An hourly GitHub Actions workflow, daily_scrape.yml, scraped listings, deployed Hosting with a FIREBASE_TOKEN secret, committed the database, and sent the digest through Gmail SMTP. There was no Firestore, and no Firebase web app was registered.

The zip leaves out env vars, including applicant details. Offline, the public/ tree from the working-tree zip can be served as static files. The scrape and the mail do not run without credentials.

What I learned

The part that outlived the idea was the clock. At archive time the hourly workflow was still live, still using Actions minutes, a Firebase CI token, and email. The note I kept says to disable that workflow before retiring the host. Nothing in that pass was deleted.

Where it went

Retired as a product. The useful copy is the Drive package. It did not move into Dawn, Bagel, or Pantheon.

Download the archive

mia-maps-archive.zip in the Unlisted sites 2026-11-13 folder. The index records 2,802,879 bytes and SHA-256 5e5c98c3672f02695647bdd07dfcc52d8acc9b337bf86f44fe1861c872148743. SUMMARY.json lists a git bundle, a working-tree zip, and a live mirror inside that package.

title: Mint
description: A private image and short-video generator. The voice note called it MIT. No GitHub repo was found.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Mint was a private generator: images, short videos, a gallery with favorites, cost logging, and social-card composites from a brand kit. The Drive README says this is what a voice note called "MIT." What it was

A signed-in studio for making pictures and short clips, closer to a private Higgsfield-style desk than to a public app. The KSM inventory had already summarized it that way. The archive README is the one that names the stack.

The README lists the jobs: generate, keep favorites, log cost, and composite a social card from a brand kit. It was private. Sign-in was restricted, and the archive does not include secrets.

The name in the voice note and the name on the host were not the same word. The README settles it: Mint, not MIT. Generation without the functions is a gallery. The archive keeps the UI and leaves the secrets out, which is the correct split.

title: Newsletter
description: The Artometrics letter: consent, a markdown composer, and batch send. The host was deleted. The note says the box source was kept for Dawn.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Newsletter was the Artometrics letter. Public signup, confirmation, compose, send, and an archive of sent issues. No GitHub repo. The box path was /workspace/newsletter-dep. The host was newsletter-510519.web.app.

What it was

A studio letter, and the inventory's first recommendation for a Dawn merge. The desk is Vite, React, and TypeScript, with Cloud Functions and rules tests. Hosting reads /__/firebase/init.json, which the note calls Spark-friendly. The desk is allowlisted. Until functions are deployed, the live desk says the back end is not enabled.

Why it was built

The magazine needed a letter that could take a signup with consent, send, and then show the issue in public. That is the feature list the inventory records, and the reason it ranks first.

How it worked

Stored consent, double opt-in, a markdown composer, a Gemini draft from notes or a URL, send in batches of 50, List-Unsubscribe, an open pixel, rewritten clicks, unique and total counts, and MCP tools for count, draft, schedule, send, and stats. Firestore (default) existed and was described as the likely home of subscribers.

Offline: npm install and npm run dev. Sending mail needs functions and is a dry run in the emulator.

The delete row on 13 Nov 2026 says Firestore was empty (no subscribers), the project delete was requested at 8:22 PM PT, the host was 404, and the source was kept on the box at /workspace/newsletter-dep for Dawn. A document export was not run.

What I learned

The letter was finished as a desk and empty as a list. No subscribers were in Firestore when it was deleted. The machinery (consent, double opt-in, batch send, unsubscribe) is what the inventory says to keep. The audience was not in the database.

Where it went

The recorded destination is Dawn, as Newsletter. The 13 Nov inventory says Dawn was not changed that night. title: Nightlight and the other small games
description: Nightlight, Questroad, Cardinal Quest, Knightmare, and the Godot toys. Archived 13 Nov 2026, then the repos and hosts were deleted.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
This note covers the small games packed on 13 Nov 2026 and then removed as standalone sites. Nightlight is the one the archive uses as the example. The others were in the same pass: the Godot port of the Artometrics site, Questroad, Spidermom rooftops, Cardinal Quest, Ashmere, Lampwick, Voltspire, Knightmare, and a 28 KB Godot test. Fernbound and Lineage have their own reports. Pantheon stayed.

On 14 Nov 2026, Artometrics/nightlight was not visible from this account. The archive index says these repos were deleted at 6:35 PM PT and the Hosting sites at 6:38 PM PT, after the Drive copies were uploaded. I am using that index and the Nightlight folder README, not a live checkout.

What they were

Nightlight was a flashlight horror walk. The folder README says "flashlight horror walk-around," web plus 3D assets, on Firebase Hosting at nightlight-510519.web.app. The bundle has 10 commits, HEAD c5b73e7f26c2 on main. Kyle used it as the example that does not fold into Dawn.

Questroad was the GPS quest on the real map, host questroad-510519.web.app, repo Artometrics/questroad. A box copy also sat at /workspace/games/waze. The index says map, GPS, and Firestore are limited offline.

Cardinal Quest was the Stanford landmark hunt, host cardinal-quest-510519.web.app, repo Artometrics/cardinal-quest. A box copy also sat at /workspace/games/stanford. The index says it is not the Cardinal book site. Live GPS was required for campus unlocks.

Knightmare was a greybox prototype. Hosts were artometrics-knightmare.web.app and knightmare-ksm.web.app, and the index says the KSM URL was a lock page only. The password was not used or recorded. Serve deploy/export over HTTP.

Spidermom rooftops was filed as far-out original IP, host spidermom-rooftops.web.app, repo Artometrics/spider-mom-rooftops. Serve the game/export folder over HTTP.

Ashmere, Lampwick, and Voltspire were Godot web exports, each with two hosts (a -510519 site and an artometrics- site). Ashmere is described as a CYOA or story-walk, with an optional fold of that idea into Dawn and a retire for the Godot build. Lampwick is filed as first-person horror, same class as Nightlight. Voltspire is filed as a retro-futurist FPS. Their Firebase projects were deleted about 6:39 PM PT.

The Godot game page was a Godot port of the Artometrics site, host artometrics-godot-510519.web.app, repo Artometrics/artometrics-godot. The index says it is not a Dawn game loop. Serve the web export over HTTP, not file://.

The Godot test was a 28 KB scratch project with no live site. Open project.godot in Godot 4.

Why they were built

The index sorts them by whether the idea could live inside something else. Questroad's GPS quests and Cardinal Quest's landmark hunt were written down as Dawn or Cardinal material. Nightlight, Lampwick, Voltspire, Spidermom, Knightmare, and the Godot site port were written down as toys that stay toys. The Godot test was a scratch file.

How they worked

Nightlight: serve site/ over HTTP. The README names a web game and 3D assets.

Questroad and Cardinal Quest: serve public/. Questroad's map and Firestore do not fully work offline. Cardinal Quest's unlocks need live GPS.

The Godot games: serve the web export over HTTP.

Knightmare: serve deploy/export.

Each deleted repo's folder holds a bundle or a working-tree zip, a live mirror where there was a site, and, for several of them, a screenshots.zip added at 8:24 PM PT. This report does not describe those pictures.

What I learned

A flashlight game is a clean test of scope. If it does not fit Dawn, the horror cousins do not fit either. The index applies that test to Lampwick in those words. The other lesson is clerical: two hosts per Godot repo, a lock page that was not the game, and a password that was never written down. The archive is the copy. The hosts are gone.

Where it went

Retired as standalone sites. Questroad's idea was filed as a fold into Dawn. Cardinal Quest's idea was filed as a Dawn location hunt or as material for the Cardinal rebuild. Ashmere's story-walk was optional for Dawn. The index does not say those folds were done. Nightlight and the horror and FPS toys were retired outright. Pantheon was not part of this delete.

title: Storefront

The shop was real enough to archive and small enough to drop. The written call was archive-only. If selling ever belongs inside Dawn, this zip is the source. It does not belong there by default.

title: Vault
description: A research shelf and a photo shelf. Heavier than the CRM, and left as a later Dawn library or an archive.
author: Kyle McAuliffe
body:
Vault was a mobile-first PWA with two shelves: research files, and photographs. No GitHub repo was found. The box path in the index is /workspace/vault-dep. The host was vault-510519.web.app.

What it was

A private library. One shelf took PDFs, EPUBs, and transcripts. The other took photos. The inventory calls the code good, and larger than Newsletter or CRM, because of Cloud Functions and embeddings.

Why it was built

The inventory describes the job as filing research so questions come back with citations, and tagging photographs so the originals can be zipped. That is the whole brief that was written down.

How it worked

Firebase project vault-510519, with Firestore (default). The research shelf filed work into collections named Cardinal, Ivory, Silica, or Artometrics, chunked and embedded the files, and answered questions with page or timestamp citations. Export was Markdown or BibTeX. The photo shelf had tags, favorites, a zip of originals, and watermark copies. There was a REST API and a small MCP server, plus rules tests.

Offline: npm install && npm run dev against emulators. Research answers need a local model or key. The index says not to delete the Firebase project.

What I learned

Citations and embeddings made a better library and a worse merge. The 13 Nov note ranks it behind Newsletter and CRM for a Dawn move, and leaves the choice as "archive only for now, or a later Dawn library." Hosting could be disabled. The project stays while Firestore is there. The index does not record a later delete.

Where it went

Archived. The optional later home is a Dawn library. That merge is not in the Dawn repo as of the 13 Nov note, which says Dawn was not changed.
